question: what is a t wave abnormality?
gt_answer: T wave abnormalities are commonly seen on the electrocardiogram (EKG: tests that record heartbeat) [11728347]. They may be harmless [11728347, 32259342] or they may predict life-threatening conditions [15842426, 32975832]. Tall or prominent T-waves may be a sign of heart attack [11992348, 2301787]. Inverted T-wave (a deep in the recorded line) is linked to coronary heart disease [32975832]. Deep inverted symmetric T-waves called "cerebral T-waves" are seen in stroke patients[34239799]. Peaked T waves are the most frequent change in patients with kidney problems [31686358].

T-wave inversion is common in heart attack and can be a sign of silent reduced blood flow to the heart muscle [22179535, 18606329, 25970951]. These abnormalities are prevalent in non-ST-segment elevation sudden heart blood-flow problems and are linked to sudden cardiac death risk [29432131, 15618066, 17897130]. Deeply inverted T-waves in Wellens' syndrome indicate critical left anterior descending artery narrowing, while T-wave alternans predict potentially fatal abnormal heart rhythms [21140289, 26603327, 23870659]. T-wave abnormalities can result from non-heart-related disease processes and are associated with early artery plaque buildup [33420509, 18606329, 16308114]. T-wave oversensing can cause inappropriate implanted defibrillator shocks, and T-wave changes can occur after extra electrical connection removal [18616439, 18709008, 28353570]. T-wave inversion is also common in thickened heart muscle disease and T-wave reversal in lead aVR is linked to sudden death risk [22179535, 21632912, 36942750].
